questions.explanation: Monitoring dashboards visualize incoming submissions, completion rates, and quality indicators so supervisors can act while fieldwork is ongoing.

questions.q: In enumerator management, why are unique enumerator IDs embedded in each submission?
options: To attribute submissions and monitor individual performance and errors
questions.explanation: Enumerator IDs let supervisors trace each record to its collector, enabling performance monitoring, error tracing, and accountability.

questions.q: What is the typical role of an 'audit' log (audit field) in SurveyCTO/ODK?
options: It records how long the enumerator spent on each question and screen events
questions.explanation: The audit metadata logs timestamps, navigation, and duration per question, helping detect rushed or fabricated interviews.

questions.q: Which appearance value renders a select_one question as a set of large, easily tappable buttons or a minimal dropdown?
questions.explanation: The 'minimal' appearance shows choices as a space-saving dropdown; appearance settings control how a question is rendered without changing its data.

questions.q: What is the main advantage of using 'cascading select' questions in a form?
options: They filter later choice lists based on earlier answers (e.g., district then village)
questions.explanation: Cascading selects use choice_filter so that selecting a state narrows the district list, and district narrows the village list, reducing errors.

questions.q: In an XLSForm 'choices' sheet, which extra column is typically used to power a cascading (filtered) select?
options: a filter column such as 'state' referenced by choice_filter
questions.explanation: Cascading selects add a filter column (e.g., state) in choices, and the survey question's choice_filter matches it against a prior answer.

questions.q: What does the XLSForm 'repeat' group (begin repeat / end repeat) allow you to do?
options: Collect the same set of questions multiple times, e.g., for each household member
questions.explanation: A repeat group lets enumerators capture a repeating roster, such as details for every member of a household, without knowing the count in advance.

questions.q: Which field-data-security practice best reduces risk if an enumerator's device is lost?
options: Storing data in plain text for easy recovery
Sharing one login across all enumerators
Using a device passcode plus encrypted forms and prompt server upload
questions.explanation: Device passcodes, form encryption, and frequent uploads minimize how much identifiable data a lost device retains and exposes.

questions.q: Why should each enumerator ideally have their own login account rather than a shared one?
options: It enables accurate attribution, individual permissions, and revocation if needed
questions.explanation: Individual accounts allow submissions to be attributed correctly and let managers grant or revoke access per person for security.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'pilot' or field test of a digital survey form before full deployment?
options: To catch skip-logic errors, translation issues, and usability problems early
questions.explanation: Piloting reveals broken skip logic, confusing wording, and device issues before they corrupt large-scale data collection.

questions.q: In the data pipeline, what is the usual sequence from field to analysis?
options: Form design, device collection, server sync, cleaning, then analysis
Cleaning, then form design, then GPS
Analysis, then form design, then collection
questions.explanation: A typical pipeline flows from form authoring to device-based collection, server upload, data cleaning/validation, and finally analysis.

questions.q: What does an API export from KoboToolbox or SurveyCTO commonly enable?
options: Programmatic, scheduled pulling of data into tools like R, Python, or Power BI
questions.explanation: REST APIs let analysts automate data extraction into statistical and BI tools, powering live dashboards and reproducible pipelines.

questions.q: Which XLSForm question type is used to capture a photograph during an interview?
questions.explanation: The 'image' type opens the camera (or gallery) to capture a photo, one of several media types alongside audio and video.

questions.q: Which XLSForm type scans a QR code or barcode, e.g., to read a beneficiary card ID?
questions.explanation: The 'barcode' type uses the device camera to scan QR codes and barcodes, reducing manual entry errors for IDs.

questions.q: What is the function of a 'note' type question in an XLSForm?
options: It displays read-only text/instructions without collecting data
questions.explanation: A 'note' shows informational or instructional text to the enumerator and does not capture any response.

questions.q: Why is 'constraint_message' recommended whenever you set a constraint?
options: It tells the enumerator why the entry was rejected and how to fix it
questions.explanation: A clear constraint_message helps enumerators understand and correct invalid entries in the field, improving data quality.

questions.q: In real-time monitoring, a sudden spike in interviews completed in unusually short durations may indicate what?
options: Possible data fabrication or rushed interviews needing review
questions.explanation: Abnormally short interview durations are a classic red flag for fabrication or skipped questions, warranting supervisor follow-up.

questions.q: What does 'server' refer to in the ODK/KoboToolbox architecture?
options: The central platform that stores form definitions and receives submissions
questions.explanation: The server (e.g., ODK Central, Kobo's server) hosts blank forms for download and collects and stores completed submissions.

questions.q: ODK Central is best described as which of the following?
options: The modern self-hosted/managed server for the ODK ecosystem
questions.explanation: ODK Central is the current server component for managing forms, users, and submissions, replacing the older ODK Aggregate.

questions.q: Which app is the standard ODK data collection client installed on Android devices?
questions.explanation: ODK Collect is the Android app enumerators use to download blank forms, fill them, and submit responses to a server.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of 'preloading' or 'server data' (e.g., a beneficiary list) into a form?
options: Enumerators can look up and confirm existing records instead of retyping them
questions.explanation: Preloaded reference data (via CSV attachments or pull-data functions) lets enumerators select existing cases, reducing entry errors and enabling follow-up.

questions.q: In SurveyCTO/ODK, what does the pulldata() function do?
options: Looks up a value from an attached CSV dataset during form filling
questions.explanation: pulldata() retrieves a field from a pre-attached CSV based on a key, enabling roster lookups and pre-filled respondent details offline.

questions.q: Why is capturing metadata like 'start' and 'end' timestamps recommended in a survey form?
options: To measure interview duration and support quality checks
questions.explanation: start/end timestamps record when the interview began and finished, enabling duration-based quality control and productivity tracking.

questions.q: What is a key data-protection reason to avoid collecting personally identifiable information (PII) you do not need?
options: Data minimization reduces harm and legal risk if a breach occurs
questions.explanation: Data minimization means collecting only necessary PII, lowering the potential harm to respondents and compliance risk if data is exposed.

questions.q: What does 'read-only' access for a data analyst on the survey server help enforce?
options: Separation of duties so analysts can view but not alter or delete raw data
questions.explanation: Role-based, read-only access follows least-privilege principles, protecting raw data integrity and audit trails.

questions.q: Which appearance setting makes a text or integer question capture handwriting or a signature?
questions.explanation: Using the 'signature' or 'draw' appearance on an image-type question lets enumerators capture a handwritten signature or sketch, e.g., for consent.

questions.q: In XLSForm, what does setting default language and multiple 'label::language' columns enable?
options: Presenting the same form in several languages selectable in the field
questions.explanation: Adding label::English, label::Hindi, etc., lets a single form support multiple languages the enumerator can switch between, key for multilingual South Asia.

questions.q: What is a recommended practice for backing up field data during multi-day fieldwork without daily connectivity?
options: Periodically export/finalize and, when possible, sync to the server and keep encrypted device backups
Email raw PII over public Wi-Fi
questions.explanation: Regular finalizing plus opportunistic encrypted syncs protect against device loss while maintaining confidentiality of unsynced records.

questions.q: Which statement about 'select_multiple' questions is correct?
options: They let a respondent choose several options from a list
questions.explanation: select_multiple lets respondents pick multiple applicable choices, and the stored value is a space-separated list of selected option names.

questions.q: When designing a data pipeline, why is a documented, reproducible cleaning script (in R/Python) preferable to manual edits in a spreadsheet?
options: It is transparent, repeatable, and preserves an auditable record of transformations
It removes the need for constraints
questions.explanation: Scripted cleaning is reproducible and auditable, so corrections can be re-run when new data arrives and every transformation is traceable, unlike ad hoc manual edits.

questions.q: Which practice best protects respondent consent in a digital survey?
options: Including a consent question with a relevant clause that ends the interview if the respondent declines
questions.explanation: A consent question tied to skip logic (relevant) ensures the interview proceeds only if the respondent agrees, documenting informed consent.

questions.q: What fundamentally distinguishes vector data from raster data in a GIS?
options: Vector uses points, lines, and polygons; raster uses a grid of cells (pixels)
Vector can only store one attribute; raster can store many
Vector is always more accurate than raster
Vector cannot be edited once created
questions.explanation: Vector data represents features as discrete geometries (points, lines, polygons), while raster data represents space as a continuous grid of equally sized cells.

questions.q: A satellite image showing land cover across a district is best described as which data model?
questions.explanation: Satellite imagery is a raster because it is composed of a grid of pixels, each holding a value such as reflectance or land-cover class.

questions.q: Which data model is generally more efficient for representing sharp administrative boundaries like district borders?
questions.explanation: Vector polygons capture crisp, well-defined boundaries precisely without the blockiness that raster cells introduce.

questions.q: In a vector dataset, what does the 'attribute table' store?
options: The pixel values of an image
The descriptive information (fields) associated with each feature
questions.explanation: The attribute table holds the non-spatial data (e.g., name, population) linked to each geometry, one row per feature.

questions.q: A coordinate reference system (CRS) is needed primarily to do what?
options: Define how locations on the curved Earth map to coordinates on a flat plane
questions.explanation: A CRS specifies the datum and projection that translate real-world positions into usable coordinates for mapping and analysis.

questions.q: Which coordinate system uses degrees of latitude and longitude on a spheroid?
questions.explanation: Geographic coordinate systems express positions in angular units (latitude/longitude) referenced to a datum like WGS84.

questions.q: What is EPSG:4326 commonly known as?
questions.explanation: EPSG:4326 is the WGS84 geographic coordinate system using decimal degrees, the default for GPS and most GeoJSON data.

questions.q: Why do all flat map projections introduce distortion?
options: Because a curved (3D) surface cannot be flattened without stretching, tearing, or shearing
Because attribute tables are too large
questions.explanation: Projecting the roughly spherical Earth onto a plane inevitably distorts some combination of area, shape, distance, or direction.

questions.q: The Mercator projection is well known for distorting which property most severely?
options: The relative area of landmasses far from the equator
questions.explanation: Mercator preserves local angles but greatly exaggerates the area of high-latitude regions like Greenland and Russia.

questions.q: For measuring true area of districts in a country, which type of projection is most appropriate?
questions.explanation: Equal-area projections preserve relative area, making them the correct choice for area-based statistical and thematic mapping.

questions.q: What does the UTM system divide the world into?
options: 60 north-south zones each 6 degrees of longitude wide
questions.explanation: The Universal Transverse Mercator system splits the globe into 60 zones of 6 degrees longitude to minimize distortion within each zone.

questions.q: Much of central and southern India falls within which UTM zone?
questions.explanation: India spans UTM zones 42N through 46N, with much of the country's centre in zones 43N and 44N.

questions.q: A shapefile is actually a set of files. Which three extensions are mandatory?
questions.explanation: A valid shapefile requires the .shp (geometry), .shx (index), and .dbf (attributes); .prj (projection) is strongly recommended but optional.

questions.q: What does a missing .prj file in a shapefile typically cause?
options: The layer's coordinate system is unknown, so it may not align with other layers
The file cannot be opened at all
questions.explanation: Without the .prj file the software does not know the CRS, often causing misalignment or requiring the user to define it manually.

questions.q: GeoJSON stores geometry using which underlying format?
questions.explanation: GeoJSON is a plain-text, human-readable format built on JSON, widely used for web mapping.

questions.q: Per the GeoJSON specification, coordinates are ordered as which of the following?
questions.explanation: GeoJSON stores coordinates as [longitude, latitude] (x, y), a common source of errors when users assume lat/long order.

questions.q: The GeoJSON specification (RFC 7946) assumes which default coordinate reference system?
questions.explanation: RFC 7946 mandates WGS84 longitude/latitude, so a compliant GeoJSON file needs no explicit CRS declaration.

questions.q: Which of these is a key advantage of GeoJSON over shapefiles for web applications?
options: It supports unlimited attribute field-name length and is natively readable by browsers/JavaScript
questions.explanation: GeoJSON is text-based, browser-friendly, and free of the shapefile's 10-character field-name and 2GB size limits.

questions.q: What is geocoding?
options: Converting text addresses or place names into geographic coordinates
questions.explanation: Geocoding matches descriptive locations (addresses, village names) to latitude/longitude coordinates for mapping.

questions.q: The reverse of geocoding, turning coordinates into a human-readable address, is called what?
questions.explanation: Reverse geocoding takes a coordinate pair and returns the nearest address or place name.

questions.q: In South Asia, a common challenge for address geocoding is which of the following?
options: Inconsistent, informal, or non-standardized addresses and multiple spellings of place names
questions.explanation: Informal addressing, transliteration variants, and duplicated village names make automated geocoding error-prone in the region.

questions.q: A choropleth map is best suited for displaying which kind of data?
options: A rate or ratio aggregated by area, such as literacy rate per district
questions.explanation: Choropleth maps shade predefined areas by a statistical value and work best with normalized rates or ratios, not raw counts.

questions.q: Why should choropleth maps generally show rates rather than raw totals?
options: Larger or more populous areas otherwise dominate simply because of size or population, misleading the reader
questions.explanation: Mapping raw counts by area conflates the phenomenon with population/area size; normalizing to a rate makes areas comparable.

questions.q: A point (dot) map is most appropriate for which purpose?
options: Showing an aggregated rate across administrative units
Showing the locations of individual discrete events or facilities
questions.explanation: Point maps mark discrete locations (e.g., each school or reported case), preserving the individual event rather than aggregating.

questions.q: The 'modifiable areal unit problem' (MAUP) refers to what?
options: Statistical results changing depending on how boundaries are drawn or aggregated
questions.explanation: MAUP describes how the same underlying data can yield different patterns depending on the zoning and scale of aggregation units.

questions.q: To display a value on a choropleth, why is the choice of class breaks (bins) important?
options: Different classification methods can dramatically change the visual pattern and message
questions.explanation: Methods like equal-interval, quantile, or natural breaks group data differently, strongly shaping how the map reads.

questions.q: An 'attribute join' (table join) in GIS links spatial features to tabular data using what?
options: A shared common field / key present in both tables
questions.explanation: A tabular join matches rows using a common key (e.g., district code) so external data can be mapped onto existing geometries.

questions.q: A common cause of a failed attribute join between a boundary layer and a data table is which of the following?
options: The map is too zoomed in
Mismatched key values, such as differing spellings or codes for the same place
Too many colors in the legend
questions.explanation: Joins fail when key fields do not match exactly (e.g., 'Bengaluru' vs 'Bangalore' or trailing spaces), leaving unmatched records.

questions.q: A 'spatial join' differs from an attribute join because it matches records based on what?
options: Their geographic relationship, such as which points fall inside which polygons
questions.explanation: A spatial join relates features by location/topology (contains, intersects, nearest) rather than by a shared attribute key.

questions.q: In South Asian data work, official codes like the LGD or census codes are valuable for joins because they do what?
options: Provide stable, unique identifiers that avoid ambiguous place-name spellings
questions.explanation: Standard administrative codes give each unit a unique, spelling-independent key, making tabular joins far more reliable.

questions.q: QGIS is best described as which of the following?
options: A free and open-source desktop GIS application
questions.explanation: QGIS is free, open-source desktop GIS software widely used in the development sector as an alternative to commercial tools.

questions.q: In QGIS, the 'Layers' panel is used primarily to do what?
options: Manage the stacking order and visibility of the datasets on the map
questions.explanation: The Layers panel controls which datasets display, their draw order, and their styling in the map canvas.

questions.q: In QGIS, what does the 'Field Calculator' allow you to do?
options: Create or update attribute values using expressions, e.g., computing a rate from two columns
questions.explanation: The Field Calculator adds or updates attribute-table fields using expressions, such as deriving population density from population and area.

questions.q: A 'buffer' operation in GIS produces what?
options: A zone of a specified distance around features (points, lines, or polygons)
questions.explanation: Buffering creates polygons a set distance around input features, useful for questions like 'population within 5 km of a clinic'.

questions.q: Remote sensing is best defined as which of the following?
options: Acquiring information about the Earth's surface without physical contact, typically via satellite or aerial sensors
questions.explanation: Remote sensing collects data about the surface from a distance using sensors on satellites, aircraft, or drones.

questions.q: In remote sensing, 'spatial resolution' refers to what?
options: The ground area represented by one pixel (e.g., 10 m or 30 m)
How often the satellite revisits a location
questions.explanation: Spatial resolution is the size of the ground area a single pixel covers; smaller cell size means finer detail.

questions.q: The time between successive satellite passes over the same location is called which resolution?
questions.explanation: Temporal resolution (revisit time) describes how frequently a satellite images the same spot, important for monitoring change.

questions.q: NDVI, derived from satellite imagery, is commonly used to assess what?
questions.explanation: The Normalized Difference Vegetation Index uses red and near-infrared bands to indicate vegetation vigour, useful in agriculture and drought monitoring.

questions.q: Landsat and Sentinel-2 are examples of what?
options: Publicly available (often free) satellite imagery programs
questions.explanation: Landsat (USGS/NASA) and Sentinel-2 (ESA) provide free, openly accessible multispectral imagery widely used in development work.

questions.q: Nighttime lights imagery is often used in development research as a proxy for what?
questions.explanation: Nighttime light intensity correlates with electrification and economic activity, offering a spatial proxy where survey data are sparse.

questions.q: When using maps for programme targeting, why should you check the vintage (date) of the boundary and population data?
options: Administrative boundaries and populations change over time, so stale data can misallocate resources
Newer data always has fewer colors
questions.explanation: Boundaries get redrawn and populations shift, so outdated layers can send resources to the wrong or mislabelled areas.

questions.q: In monitoring and evaluation (M&E), mapping intervention sites against outcome indicators primarily helps do what?
options: Replace the need for baseline data
Reveal spatial patterns, coverage gaps, and possible geographic correlations
questions.explanation: Spatial M&E highlights where coverage is thin and where outcomes cluster, though it shows correlation, not proof of causation.

questions.q: A map showing raw case counts by district can mislead targeting because it may do what?
options: Highlight populous districts even if their per-capita rate is low
questions.explanation: Raw counts track population size, so high-population districts appear worst even when their rate is average, distorting need-based targeting.

questions.q: Which practice best supports 'map honesty' when designing a choropleth?
options: Truncating the legend to exaggerate differences
Clearly labeling the classification method, data source, and units
Using a rainbow palette for sequential data
questions.explanation: Transparent labeling of data source, units, and classification lets readers judge the map fairly rather than being misled.

questions.q: For a sequential quantitative variable (e.g., poverty rate low to high), which color scheme is most appropriate?
options: A single-hue sequential ramp from light to dark
A qualitative scheme of unrelated hues
A diverging red-white-blue scheme centered on zero
questions.explanation: Sequential single-hue ramps intuitively encode magnitude order, whereas qualitative or diverging schemes imply the wrong data structure.

questions.q: A diverging color scheme is most appropriate for data that has what characteristic?
options: A meaningful midpoint with values deviating in two directions (e.g., above/below average)
questions.explanation: Diverging schemes emphasize deviation from a critical midpoint (like zero change or the mean) in two directions.

questions.q: Why is using a rainbow (spectral) palette for ordered numeric data discouraged in good map design?
options: The hue order is not perceptually uniform and can create false boundaries and mislead readers
It only works in raster data
questions.explanation: Rainbow ramps have uneven perceptual steps and abrupt hue shifts that fabricate patterns and hinder colorblind readers.

questions.q: Which essential map element tells readers the relationship between map distance and ground distance?
questions.explanation: A scale bar communicates real-world distance and remains valid even if the map is resized, unlike a stated ratio alone.

questions.q: For accessibility, a well-designed thematic map should ideally do which of the following?
options: Use colorblind-safe palettes and not encode information by color alone
questions.explanation: Colorblind-safe palettes plus redundant cues (patterns, labels) ensure the map is readable by people with color-vision deficiency.

questions.q: When integrating a village-level survey with a district boundary layer for mapping, the FIRST thing to verify is what?
options: That both datasets share a common, correctly matched key or are in a compatible CRS for spatial joining
That the map has a north arrow
That the file is under 1 MB
questions.explanation: Correct data linkage requires matching keys (for tabular joins) or a shared CRS (for spatial joins) before any styling matters.

questions.q: In supervised learning, what does the model learn from?
options: Labeled examples pairing inputs with known outputs
questions.explanation: Supervised learning trains on labeled data where each input is paired with its correct output so the model can learn the mapping.

questions.q: A program that groups households into clusters based on spending patterns without any predefined categories is an example of:
questions.explanation: Clustering without predefined labels is a classic unsupervised learning task that discovers structure in unlabeled data.

questions.q: Predicting whether a loan applicant will default (yes/no) is best described as a:
questions.explanation: Predicting a discrete category such as default/no-default is a classification problem.

questions.q: Estimating a household's monthly income in rupees from survey features is an example of:
questions.explanation: Predicting a continuous numeric value like income is a regression task.

questions.q: In machine learning, 'features' refer to:
options: The correct answers the model must predict
The measurable input variables used to make predictions
questions.explanation: Features are the input variables (attributes) the model uses to make its predictions.

questions.q: In a dataset predicting crop yield, the 'label' would be:
options: The actual crop yield being predicted
questions.explanation: The label is the target output the model is trained to predict, here the crop yield.

questions.q: Why is a dataset typically split into training, validation, and test sets?
options: To tune and evaluate the model on data it did not train on
To reduce the total amount of data needed
To remove all missing values automatically
questions.explanation: Separate validation and test sets let you tune and then honestly assess performance on unseen data.

questions.q: The test set should be used to:
options: Increase the size of the training data
Provide a final, unbiased estimate of performance
questions.explanation: The test set is held out until the end to give an unbiased estimate of how the model generalizes.

questions.q: Overfitting occurs when a model:
options: Performs poorly on both training and new data
Is too simple to capture any pattern
Has too few parameters to learn
Memorizes training data but generalizes poorly to new data
questions.explanation: Overfitting means the model fits training noise and details, so it does well in training but poorly on new data.

questions.q: Which is a common sign of overfitting?
options: Low accuracy on both training and test sets
Identical accuracy on training and test sets
The model refusing to train at all
High training accuracy but much lower test accuracy
questions.explanation: A large gap between high training accuracy and low test accuracy is a hallmark of overfitting.

questions.q: Underfitting is best described as a model that:
options: Fits the training data too closely
Is too simple to capture the underlying pattern
Performs perfectly on the test set
questions.explanation: Underfitting happens when a model is too simple, performing poorly even on training data.

questions.q: Accuracy as an evaluation metric measures:
options: The proportion of all predictions that are correct
Only the proportion of positive cases found
questions.explanation: Accuracy is the fraction of total predictions (both classes) that the model got right.

questions.q: Precision answers the question:
options: Of all actual positives, how many did we find?
Of all cases we predicted positive, how many were truly positive?
How many cases did we predict overall?
How fast does the model make predictions?
questions.explanation: Precision is the fraction of predicted positives that are actually positive.

questions.q: Recall answers the question:
options: Of all predicted positives, how many were correct?
Of all actual positives, how many did the model correctly identify?
What fraction of all predictions were correct?
How balanced are the two classes?
questions.explanation: Recall (sensitivity) is the fraction of true positives that the model successfully identified.

questions.q: Why can accuracy be misleading on an imbalanced dataset (e.g. 1% of people have a rare disease)?
options: Because accuracy cannot be computed on imbalanced data
Accuracy always equals recall on imbalanced data
Imbalanced data makes accuracy always low
A model predicting 'no disease' for everyone scores 99% accuracy while catching no cases
questions.explanation: With rare positives, always predicting the majority class gives high accuracy but useless recall.

questions.q: For a screening tool where missing a true case is very costly, which metric matters most?
questions.explanation: High recall minimizes false negatives, which is critical when missing a real case is costly.

questions.q: The F1 score is useful because it:
options: Balances precision and recall into a single number
Counts the number of features used
questions.explanation: The F1 score is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, balancing the two.

questions.q: Bias in a machine learning model most often originates from:
options: Training data that reflects existing societal inequities or is unrepresentative
Using continuous rather than discrete labels
questions.explanation: Models learn from data, so unrepresentative or historically biased data produces biased predictions.

questions.q: A hiring model trained on past hires that favored one gender is likely to:
options: Reproduce or amplify the historical bias
Improve fairness over time on its own
questions.explanation: Models trained on biased historical outcomes tend to perpetuate and even amplify that bias.

questions.q: Which practice helps detect unfair outcomes across groups in a model?
options: Disaggregating performance metrics by subgroup (e.g. gender, caste, region)
questions.explanation: Evaluating metrics separately for each subgroup reveals disparities hidden by aggregate scores.

questions.q: Removing a sensitive attribute like caste from the features guarantees a fair model. This statement is:
options: False, because proxy variables can still encode the attribute
True, because the model cannot see the attribute
False, only when data is balanced
questions.explanation: Correlated proxy features (e.g. location, name, income) can reintroduce the sensitive attribute indirectly.

questions.q: A large language model (LLM) is primarily trained to:
options: Predict the next token in text sequences at scale
questions.explanation: LLMs are trained on next-token prediction over vast text corpora, learning language patterns.

questions.q: An LLM 'hallucination' refers to:
options: The model producing fluent but factually incorrect or fabricated output
questions.explanation: A hallucination is confident, plausible-sounding output that is factually wrong or invented.

questions.q: Responsible use of an LLM to draft a policy brief should include:
options: Assuming all outputs are always accurate
Human verification of facts and citations before use
Hiding that AI was used regardless of context
questions.explanation: LLM outputs can be wrong, so human fact-checking and appropriate disclosure are essential.

questions.q: When is machine learning generally NOT the right tool for a development problem?
options: When there is abundant relevant historical data
When patterns are complex and hard to specify manually
When the problem is simple, rules are clear, and little data exists
When predictions must scale to millions of records
questions.explanation: For simple, well-understood problems with clear rules and scarce data, a rule-based approach beats ML.

questions.q: A key data requirement before building a supervised model is:
options: Sufficient, representative, and reasonably accurate labeled data
questions.explanation: Supervised learning needs enough labeled, representative data that reflects the real deployment setting.

questions.q: 'Human-in-the-loop' in an ML system means:
options: Humans are removed once the model is deployed
The model trains without any human data
Only the model makes final decisions
Humans review, correct, or approve model outputs at key points
questions.explanation: Human-in-the-loop keeps people involved to review or override the model, especially for high-stakes decisions.

questions.q: For a high-stakes decision like flagging a child for protective services, the appropriate ML role is usually:
options: A decision-support aid with a human making the final call
Fully automated decision with no human review
questions.explanation: In sensitive, high-stakes contexts, ML should support human judgment rather than replace it.

questions.q: Data leakage in model building refers to:
options: Information from the test set or future improperly influencing training
questions.explanation: Data leakage occurs when information unavailable at prediction time leaks into training, inflating performance.

questions.q: Which is an example of unsupervised learning?
options: Grouping villages into segments by socioeconomic similarity
Predicting exam scores from study hours
Classifying emails as spam or not
questions.explanation: Grouping without predefined labels is clustering, an unsupervised technique.

questions.q: A confusion matrix is used to:
options: Summarize correct and incorrect predictions by class
questions.explanation: A confusion matrix tabulates true/false positives and negatives to reveal where a classifier errs.

questions.q: A 'false negative' in a disease-screening model is:
options: A sick person missed and labeled healthy
A healthy person flagged as sick
questions.explanation: A false negative is a true positive case the model failed to detect, labeling it negative.

questions.q: A 'false positive' in fraud detection is:
options: A legitimate transaction wrongly flagged as fraud
questions.explanation: A false positive is a negative case incorrectly predicted as positive.

questions.q: Cross-validation is used mainly to:
options: Estimate model performance more reliably using multiple train/validation splits
Increase the raw size of the dataset
Replace the need for a test set entirely
questions.explanation: Cross-validation rotates the validation split across folds to give a more robust performance estimate.

questions.q: Which best describes 'generalization' in ML?
options: Performing well on new, unseen data
Running on many computers at once
questions.explanation: Generalization is the model's ability to perform well on data it has not seen before.

questions.q: Feature engineering refers to:
options: Creating or transforming input variables to improve model learning
Increasing the number of test examples
questions.explanation: Feature engineering shapes raw data into informative inputs that help models learn better.

questions.q: Which statement about training data representativeness is correct?
options: A model works equally well on any population regardless of training data
A model trained on urban data may perform poorly when applied to rural populations
Larger data always removes representativeness concerns
questions.explanation: Models can fail on populations underrepresented in training data, so representativeness is crucial.

questions.q: Regularization techniques are primarily used to:
options: Reduce overfitting by penalizing model complexity
questions.explanation: Regularization discourages overly complex models, helping reduce overfitting.

questions.q: Which scenario is best suited to a classification model?
options: Sorting citizen complaints into department categories
questions.explanation: Assigning items to discrete categories (departments) is a classification task.

questions.q: A major risk of deploying an ML model without ongoing monitoring is:
options: The model becomes faster over time
Model drift as real-world data changes, degrading performance
questions.explanation: As populations and behaviors change, model drift can silently erode performance without monitoring.

questions.q: Which is a legitimate reason to prefer a simpler, interpretable model over a complex one in development work?
options: Simpler models are always more accurate
Stakeholders and affected people can understand and contest the decisions
Complex models cannot be trained on real data
Interpretability is required by all algorithms
questions.explanation: Interpretable models support accountability, letting people understand and challenge decisions.

questions.q: Informed consent for using personal data in an ML project matters because:
options: People have a right to know and agree to how their data is used
It removes the need for a test set
questions.explanation: Ethical and often legal use of personal data requires people's informed consent.

questions.q: The concept of 'ground truth' in ML refers to:
options: The verified correct labels against which predictions are compared
questions.explanation: Ground truth is the reliable, correct answer used to train and evaluate models.

questions.q: Which is a data-quality issue that can undermine a model?
options: Systematic missing values correlated with the outcome
questions.explanation: Missingness that correlates with the outcome biases what the model learns and its predictions.

questions.q: Precision and recall often trade off because:
options: Making the model flag more cases raises recall but can lower precision
They are unrelated to the decision threshold
questions.explanation: Loosening the threshold catches more positives (higher recall) but admits more false positives (lower precision).

questions.q: When labeled data is scarce but unlabeled data is plentiful, a reasonable approach is:
options: Use only the test set for training
Consider semi-supervised methods or investing in careful labeling
questions.explanation: Semi-supervised learning or targeted labeling can leverage abundant unlabeled data effectively.

questions.q: A responsible AI practice when using an LLM chatbot for citizen services is to:
options: Let it give final legal rulings
Never log or review its answers
Provide clear disclaimers and escalation paths to humans
questions.explanation: Users should know they are talking to AI and be able to reach a human for consequential matters.

questions.q: Which best illustrates 'proxy discrimination' in a model?
options: Using rainfall to predict crop yield
Using postal code, which correlates with ethnicity, to make lending decisions
Using age to predict school grade
Using height to estimate shoe size
questions.explanation: A neutral-seeming feature like postal code can act as a proxy for a protected attribute, causing discrimination.

questions.q: Before automating a decision with ML, a key ethical question is:
options: How many colors the dashboard uses
What harm occurs if the model is wrong and who is accountable
questions.explanation: Assessing potential harms and accountability is essential before automating consequential decisions.

questions.q: A model reports 95% accuracy but only 20% recall on detecting malnutrition cases. The most reasonable interpretation is:
options: The model is excellent and ready to deploy
The model misses most actual cases despite high overall accuracy
Recall is irrelevant for health screening
questions.explanation: Low recall means most true malnutrition cases are missed, so high accuracy is misleading here.

questions.q: What does 'PII' stand for in data protection?
questions.explanation: PII refers to any information that can be used to identify a specific individual, such as name, ID number, or phone number.

questions.q: Which of the following is generally considered 'sensitive personal data' requiring extra protection?
options: The city where an office is located
A person's health condition or caste
The date a report was published
questions.explanation: Health, caste, religion, sexual orientation, and biometric data are sensitive categories that can cause serious harm if exposed.

questions.q: What is the core difference between anonymisation and pseudonymisation?
options: They are identical processes with different names
Pseudonymisation is permanent while anonymisation is reversible
Anonymisation irreversibly removes identifiability; pseudonymisation replaces identifiers with codes that can still be re-linked
Anonymisation only applies to numbers, pseudonymisation to text
questions.explanation: Truly anonymised data cannot be traced back to an individual, whereas pseudonymised data can be re-identified using a separate key.

questions.q: The principle of 'data minimisation' means an organisation should:
options: Store all data in the smallest possible file format
Minimise the number of staff who collect data
Delete all data after one year regardless of need
Collect only the data actually needed for the stated purpose
questions.explanation: Data minimisation limits collection to what is necessary and relevant for the specified purpose, reducing risk and burden.

questions.q: 'Purpose limitation' requires that personal data:
options: Is used only for the specific purposes for which it was collected
Is limited to one gigabyte per beneficiary
Serves only the organisation's fundraising goals
Is collected only during working hours
questions.explanation: Purpose limitation prohibits using data for new, incompatible purposes without fresh consent or lawful basis.

questions.q: Under India's Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act 2023, the individual whose data is processed is called the:
questions.explanation: The DPDP Act uses 'Data Principal' for the individual and 'Data Fiduciary' for the entity determining the purpose of processing.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, the entity that determines the purpose and means of processing personal data is the:
questions.explanation: The 'Data Fiduciary' is the counterpart of the GDPR 'controller' and bears primary responsibility for lawful processing.

questions.q: For informed consent to be valid, it must generally be:
options: Given verbally only and never recorded
Signed by a community leader on behalf of everyone
questions.explanation: Valid consent requires a genuine, informed, and clear affirmative choice by the individual, not silence or coercion.

questions.q: A survey enumerator collects Aadhaar numbers 'in case they are useful later.' Which principle does this most directly violate?
questions.explanation: Collecting data with no defined, necessary purpose violates both minimisation and purpose limitation.

questions.q: Which is the strongest technical safeguard for protecting data confidentiality during transfer?
options: Renaming the file to hide its contents
Sending it in a password in the email body
Compressing the file into a ZIP
questions.explanation: Encryption in transit protects data as it moves across networks, unlike obscurity tactics that offer no real security.

questions.q: 'Access control' in data security primarily ensures that:
options: The office door is locked at night
Data loads quickly for all users
Only authorised people can view or modify specific data
Everyone in the organisation can see all data
questions.explanation: Access control restricts data access based on roles and need-to-know, limiting exposure of sensitive information.

questions.q: The 'principle of least privilege' means:
options: Junior staff should never handle data
Privileges are granted only to managers
Everyone gets read-only access by default
Users get the minimum access rights needed to do their job
questions.explanation: Least privilege minimises risk by ensuring each user can access only what their specific tasks require.

questions.q: What is a 'data breach'?
options: Unauthorised access, disclosure, loss, or alteration of personal data
A scheduled backup of a database
The lawful sharing of data with a partner under agreement
A survey with a low response rate
questions.explanation: A breach is any security incident leading to unauthorised or accidental compromise of personal data.

questions.q: The first priority immediately after discovering a data breach should be to:
options: Publicly announce it on social media
Contain the breach and stop further data loss
Delete all logs to avoid embarrassment
Wait to see if anyone notices
questions.explanation: Containment limits ongoing harm; deleting logs would destroy evidence and hamper investigation and notification duties.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, in the event of a personal data breach, the Data Fiduciary must:
options: Notify only its internal board of directors
Do nothing unless the breach exceeds 10,000 records
Notify the Data Protection Board and affected Data Principals
questions.explanation: The Act requires notifying both the Data Protection Board of India and affected individuals of a breach.

questions.q: A 'do-no-harm' approach to data on vulnerable groups requires that:
options: Data on vulnerable groups is always published openly for transparency
Consent forms are skipped to save time
Potential harms to individuals and communities are assessed before collection and sharing
questions.explanation: Do-no-harm means anticipating and mitigating risks such as stigma, targeting, or reprisal before working with sensitive populations.

questions.q: Publishing a dataset with village name, gender, age, and disability status could enable re-identification through:
options: Combining quasi-identifiers to single out an individual
questions.explanation: Even without direct identifiers, combinations of quasi-identifiers can uniquely pinpoint individuals in small populations.

questions.q: 'Algorithmic bias' in an AI decision system most often arises from:
options: Training data that reflects existing social inequalities
Writing code in an old programming language
questions.explanation: Models learn patterns from historical data, so biased or unrepresentative data reproduces and can amplify discrimination.

questions.q: A beneficiary-targeting algorithm systematically excludes women from a benefits scheme. The most appropriate ethical response is to:
options: Trust the algorithm because it is objective and mathematical
Increase the dataset size without checking for bias
Audit the model for bias and add fairness safeguards and human oversight
Remove the gender field and assume the problem is solved
questions.explanation: Automated systems must be audited for discriminatory outcomes, with human review and correction where harm occurs.

questions.q: A 'data sharing agreement' between two organisations should primarily specify:
options: The favourite colour of each organisation
Only the names of the CEOs
The office rent of each party
Purpose, permitted uses, security measures, retention, and responsibilities
questions.explanation: A sound data sharing agreement defines lawful purpose, safeguards, retention, and accountability for shared data.

questions.q: Which practice best supports 'purpose limitation' when reusing an old dataset for a new study?
options: Checking whether the new use is compatible with the original consent, and seeking fresh consent if not
Using the data freely because it already exists
Selling the data to fund the new study
Assuming consent transfers automatically to any future use
questions.explanation: Reuse for a materially different purpose typically requires assessing compatibility and often obtaining renewed consent.

questions.q: Encrypting data 'at rest' means:
options: Data is encrypted only while being typed
Data stored on disks or databases is encrypted when not in use
questions.explanation: Encryption at rest protects stored data so that stolen drives or databases remain unreadable without keys.

questions.q: A 'Data Protection Impact Assessment' (DPIA) is used to:
options: Calculate the financial profit of a data project
Test whether a database loads fast enough
Identify and mitigate privacy risks before a high-risk processing activity
Decide staff salaries in the data team
questions.explanation: A DPIA systematically evaluates and reduces privacy risks before launching high-risk data processing.

questions.q: Obtaining consent from children under the DPDP Act 2023 generally requires:
options: No consent because children's data is exempt
Consent from the child's school only
Consent from any adult in the household
Verifiable consent from a parent or lawful guardian
questions.explanation: The Act requires verifiable parental/guardian consent for processing personal data of children (under 18).

questions.q: Which is an example of good 'data retention' practice?
options: Deleting or anonymising personal data once the purpose is fulfilled
Keeping all raw data forever, just in case
Retaining data based on how much storage is free
questions.explanation: Storage limitation requires keeping personal data only as long as needed for the stated purpose.

questions.q: A partner requests your beneficiary list 'to explore future collaboration.' The most privacy-protective response is to:
options: Send the full list immediately to be helpful
Decline to share identifiable data without a defined purpose and agreement, offering aggregate data if useful
Share it if the partner promises to be careful
Post the list on a shared drive open to both teams
questions.explanation: Sharing identifiable data needs a lawful, specific purpose and safeguards; aggregate data avoids exposing individuals.

questions.q: The main privacy risk of collecting GPS location of survey respondents' homes is that it:
options: Can directly re-identify and physically locate vulnerable individuals
questions.explanation: Precise geolocation is a strong identifier that can expose individuals to targeting or reprisal, especially vulnerable groups.

questions.q: 'Informed' in informed consent specifically means participants understand:
options: Only the name of the organisation
Just the length of the survey
What data is collected, why, how it will be used, and who will see it
questions.explanation: Being informed means grasping the nature, purpose, use, sharing, and risks of the data collection before agreeing.

questions.q: Which of these is NOT a valid lawful basis for processing personal data (in most frameworks)?
options: Because the data is interesting to have
Performance of a contract with the individual
questions.explanation: Mere curiosity or convenience is not a lawful basis; processing needs consent, legal obligation, contract, or similar grounds.

questions.q: Sharing a spreadsheet of HIV-positive patients over unencrypted email is problematic mainly because:
options: The spreadsheet might be formatted incorrectly
Highly sensitive data is exposed and could cause severe stigma or harm
Email is slower than a phone call
The file might be too large to send
questions.explanation: Sensitive health data must be strongly protected; exposure can lead to discrimination, violence, or loss of livelihood.

questions.q: A 'privacy by design' approach means:
options: Adding a privacy policy page after launch
Designing a logo that looks trustworthy
Building privacy protections into systems and processes from the start
Letting users opt out only after a breach
questions.explanation: Privacy by design embeds data protection into the default architecture and workflow rather than bolting it on later.

questions.q: The safest way to store passwords for a data system is to:
options: Keep them in a shared spreadsheet
Write them on a whiteboard for the team
Store them in plain text but in a hidden folder
Store them as salted cryptographic hashes, never in plain text
questions.explanation: Salted hashing ensures that even if the store is breached, actual passwords cannot be easily recovered.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, a Data Principal has the right to:
options: Access, correct, and request erasure of their personal data
Demand payment for every use of their data
Access other people's personal data freely
questions.explanation: The Act grants rights of access, correction, completion, updating, and erasure, plus grievance redress.

questions.q: A 'Significant Data Fiduciary' under the DPDP Act 2023 may be required to:
options: Stop collecting any personal data at all
Appoint a Data Protection Officer and conduct independent audits
questions.explanation: Entities designated as Significant Data Fiduciaries face extra duties like appointing a DPO and periodic audits.

questions.q: Which action best reduces re-identification risk before publishing survey microdata?
options: Aggregating small cells and removing/generalising quasi-identifiers
questions.explanation: Suppressing small cells and generalising quasi-identifiers (k-anonymity techniques) lowers re-identification risk.

questions.q: The concept of 'purpose creep' (function creep) refers to:
options: A survey that takes too long to complete
Data that degrades in quality over time
Data collected for one purpose gradually being used for unrelated purposes
questions.explanation: Function/purpose creep is the incremental drift of data use beyond the original consented purpose.

questions.q: When a consent form is written only in English for a community that speaks Bengali, the consent is likely:
options: Not truly informed, because participants may not understand it
Valid if a staff member signs it too
Only a formality with no ethical weight
questions.explanation: Consent must be understood in a language the participant comprehends; otherwise it is not genuinely informed.

questions.q: 'Data anonymisation' can fail when:
options: The data is stored on a fast server
External datasets can be linked to re-identify individuals
The dataset is very small in file size
The data is backed up regularly
questions.explanation: Linkage attacks combine anonymised data with other datasets to re-identify people, undermining anonymisation.

questions.q: Which is the best example of applying 'do-no-harm' when reporting on a trafficking survivors' programme?
options: Publishing individual survivor names to raise awareness
Aggregating data and omitting details that could identify survivors
Including exact home addresses in the report
questions.explanation: Protecting identities through aggregation prevents re-traumatisation, stigma, and safety risks for survivors.

questions.q: A key ethical concern with using AI facial recognition on beneficiaries is:
options: It makes reports look more modern
It collects immutable biometric data with high risk of surveillance and misuse
questions.explanation: Biometrics cannot be changed if compromised, and facial recognition enables intrusive surveillance and error-driven exclusion.

questions.q: The purpose of 'audit logs' in a data system is to:
options: Record who accessed or changed data and when, for accountability
Store backup copies of the database
questions.explanation: Audit logs provide traceability, helping detect misuse and support investigation after incidents.

questions.q: Which statement about consent is correct?
options: Once given, consent is permanent and irrevocable
Consent can generally be withdrawn by the individual at any time
Consent given to one organisation covers all others
Consent must always be given in writing to any degree
questions.explanation: Individuals retain the right to withdraw consent, after which processing based on that consent should stop.

questions.q: A responsible data practice when a laptop with beneficiary data is lost is to:
options: Buy a new laptop and say nothing
Assume the data is safe because there was a login password
Report the incident, assess the breach, and notify affected people/authorities as required
Blame the staff member and close the matter
questions.explanation: A lost device with personal data is a potential breach requiring assessment, containment, and notification duties.

questions.q: 'Aggregation' protects privacy by:
options: Reporting data in grouped totals rather than individual records
questions.explanation: Aggregated statistics reveal patterns without exposing identifiable individual-level information.

questions.q: Under the DPDP Act 2023, cross-border transfer of personal data is:
options: Permitted except to countries the government restricts by notification
Unregulated with no restrictions at all
questions.explanation: The Act allows transfers by default but empowers the government to restrict transfers to specified (blacklisted) countries.

questions.q: The most privacy-respectful way to seek feedback from beneficiaries is to:
options: Require full name, phone, and Aadhaar for every response
Offer an anonymous option and collect only necessary identifiers
Publish all responses with names attached
Record video of each respondent without asking
questions.explanation: Minimising identifiers and enabling anonymity encourages honest feedback while reducing privacy risk.

questions.q: 'Data sovereignty' most commonly refers to the idea that:
options: Data belongs to whoever has the fastest computer
Only governments may hold any data
Data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected or stored
questions.explanation: Data sovereignty means data is governed by the legal jurisdiction in which it resides, affecting cross-border handling.

questions.q: An M&E team wants to link datasets using a person's phone number as a common key. The main privacy risk is that:
options: Phone numbers are hard to type
Phone numbers change too often to be useful
A direct identifier is retained across datasets, increasing exposure and re-identification
questions.explanation: Using a direct identifier as a linkage key keeps individuals identifiable across systems, raising breach and misuse risk.

questions.q: A hallmark of 'meaningful transparency' with data subjects is:
options: A clear, accessible privacy notice explaining data use in plain language
A 40-page legal document no one can read
Not mentioning data collection at all
Telling people only after the project ends
questions.explanation: Transparency requires accessible, understandable information about what data is collected and how it is used.

questions.q: Which combination best reflects a mature responsible-data culture in an organisation?
options: Buying the most expensive software available
Clear policies, staff training, minimisation, security controls, and accountability
Collecting as much data as possible for flexibility
Relying only on one IT person to handle everything
questions.explanation: Responsible data practice is systemic: policy, training, minimisation, security, and accountability together protect people.

questions.q: In the FAIR data principles, what does the 'F' stand for?
questions.explanation: FAIR stands for Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable: the 'F' means data should be easy to locate via persistent identifiers and rich metadata.

questions.q: A monitoring team names files 'survey_final.xlsx', 'survey_final2.xlsx', 'survey_final_FINAL.xlsx'. What is the most robust fix?
options: Add the author's initials to each name
Store all versions in one folder
questions.explanation: ISO-dated, zero-padded version numbers sort chronologically and eliminate ambiguous 'final' labels that don't convey which copy is authoritative.

questions.q: What is the primary purpose of a data dictionary?
options: To document each variable's name, type, allowed values, and meaning
questions.explanation: A data dictionary defines every variable (its name, data type, permitted values, and description) so others can correctly interpret and reuse the dataset.

questions.q: In Git, what does a 'commit' represent?
options: A request to merge two branches
A remote copy of the repository
A saved snapshot of changes with a message and identifier
questions.explanation: A commit records a snapshot of tracked changes at a point in time, along with a message and a unique hash identifying it in the project history.

questions.q: What does 'ETL' stand for in data pipeline work?
questions.explanation: ETL means Extract data from sources, Transform it into a clean usable form, then Load it into a destination such as a database or warehouse.

questions.q: Why is a script preferred over manual copy-paste steps for cleaning data?
options: Scripts run faster on any hardware
Scripts make the process reproducible and auditable
Scripts remove the need for a data dictionary
questions.explanation: A script captures each step in code, so the same cleaning can be re-run identically and reviewed, whereas manual edits leave no reliable trace.

questions.q: What is the recommended '3-2-1' rule for backups?
options: 3 copies, on 2 media types, with 1 off-site
questions.explanation: The 3-2-1 rule advises keeping three copies of data on two different media, with at least one stored off-site to survive local disasters.

questions.q: Which file format is most appropriate for sharing tabular open data for maximum interoperability?
questions.explanation: CSV is a non-proprietary, widely readable plain-text format that, paired with a documented schema, supports the interoperability FAIR principles call for.

questions.q: What is 'version control' primarily used for?
options: Tracking changes to files over time and enabling collaboration
Restricting who can read a file
questions.explanation: Version control systems like Git track every change, who made it and when, allowing rollback and coordinated collaboration.

questions.q: In FAIR, what does 'Interoperable' mean for a dataset?
options: It works only within one organization
It uses standard formats and vocabularies so systems can combine it with other data
It is stored on interoperable hardware
It can be edited by anyone
questions.explanation: Interoperability means using shared formats, standards, and controlled vocabularies so the data can be integrated with other datasets and tools.

questions.q: What does a '.gitignore' file do?
options: Specifies files Git should not track
Hides the repository from search engines
questions.explanation: A .gitignore file lists patterns for files and folders, such as secrets or large temp files, that Git should exclude from tracking.

questions.q: Why should personally identifiable information (PII) be separated from analysis datasets?
options: Because PII cannot be stored in CSV
To reduce disclosure risk and support safe data sharing
questions.explanation: Separating direct identifiers into a restricted linkage file lets analysts work with de-identified data, lowering the risk if the analysis set is shared or breached.

questions.q: What is 'data provenance'?
options: The documented origin and history of how data was collected and transformed
The physical location of a server
The encryption method used on a file
questions.explanation: Provenance records where data came from and every processing step applied, which is essential for trust and reproducibility.

questions.q: A folder structure with 'raw/', 'processed/', and 'output/' subfolders supports which principle?
options: Never modifying raw data and keeping a clear processing flow
questions.explanation: Separating raw, processed, and output data enforces the rule that original data is never edited in place, making the pipeline traceable and reproducible.

questions.q: What is a 'schema' in the context of a dataset?
options: A definition of the structure: columns, types, and constraints
questions.explanation: A schema formally describes a dataset's structure: the fields, their data types, and rules like uniqueness or allowed ranges.

questions.q: Which practice best ensures a data analysis is reproducible by others?
options: Emailing the final chart as an image
Describing the steps verbally in a meeting
Sharing the code, data, and environment specification together
questions.explanation: Reproducibility requires that others can re-run the exact code on the same data with the same software environment to obtain the same results.

questions.q: What does 'idempotent' mean for a data pipeline step?
options: Running it multiple times produces the same result as running it once
It requires manual approval each run
questions.explanation: An idempotent step yields the same end state no matter how many times it runs, which prevents duplicated or corrupted data on re-runs.

questions.q: Why is a persistent identifier (like a DOI) valuable for a published dataset?
options: It provides a stable, citable link even if the storage location changes
It prevents anyone from downloading it
questions.explanation: A DOI is a permanent identifier that resolves to a dataset regardless of URL changes, supporting the 'Findable' FAIR principle and citation.

questions.q: What is the main risk of doing data cleaning directly in a spreadsheet by hand?
options: It is always slower than coding
The steps are not recorded, so the process cannot be reproduced or audited
It automatically deletes the raw data
questions.explanation: Manual spreadsheet edits leave no log of what changed, making the work impossible to reproduce, verify, or correct systematically.

questions.q: In Git, what is a 'branch'?
options: A separate line of development that can be merged back later
questions.explanation: A branch is an independent line of work allowing changes to be developed in isolation and later merged into the main line.

questions.q: What does 'data governance' primarily establish?
options: Policies, roles, and standards for how data is managed and used
questions.explanation: Data governance defines the rules, responsibilities, and standards for data quality, security, access, and lifecycle across an organization.

questions.q: Why should date fields use the ISO 8601 format (YYYY-MM-DD)?
options: It is unambiguous and sorts correctly as text
It is required by all spreadsheets
It hides the year for privacy
questions.explanation: ISO 8601 avoids day/month confusion across regions and sorts chronologically when treated as plain text, improving data quality.

questions.q: What is 'metadata'?
options: The largest table in a database
Data that describes other data, such as its source, format, and collection date
questions.explanation: Metadata is descriptive information about a dataset (its origin, structure, meaning, and context) enabling discovery and correct reuse.

questions.q: Which is a core benefit of automating a recurring monthly report pipeline?
options: It removes the need for any documentation
It eliminates the need for backups
It reduces manual errors and frees staff time for analysis
questions.explanation: Automation runs the same steps consistently each cycle, cutting human error and repetitive effort so staff can focus on interpretation.

questions.q: What is a 'merge conflict' in Git?
options: When competing changes to the same lines must be reconciled manually
questions.explanation: A merge conflict occurs when two branches change the same part of a file differently, requiring a person to choose or combine the changes.

questions.q: Under FAIR, what does 'Accessible' specifically emphasize?
options: Data must always be free of charge
Data and metadata are retrievable via a standard protocol, with clear access conditions
Data must be public to everyone
Data must be stored on one server
questions.explanation: Accessible means data can be retrieved by a standard, open protocol and that access conditions (including authentication) are clearly stated, not that it must be open.

questions.q: What is the purpose of a 'README' file in a data project?
options: To orient users on the project's contents, structure, and how to use it
questions.explanation: A README gives newcomers an overview of the project: what the files are, how they relate, and how to run or reproduce the work.

questions.q: Which approach best protects against accidental overwriting of the original survey data?
options: Editing the raw file and saving often
Deleting old versions to save space
Keeping raw data read-only and working on copies
questions.explanation: Marking raw data read-only and never editing it directly guarantees an untouched source of truth to fall back on.

questions.q: What is a 'data pipeline'?
options: A series of automated steps that move and transform data from source to destination
questions.explanation: A data pipeline is a sequence of processing steps, often automated, that ingest, transform, and deliver data to where it is used.

questions.q: Why are checksums (e.g., MD5/SHA-256) used when transferring or archiving files?
options: To verify the file was not altered or corrupted
questions.explanation: A checksum is a fingerprint of file contents; comparing it before and after transfer confirms the data arrived intact and unmodified.

questions.q: What does 'reproducible workflow' most directly require?
options: That only one analyst ever touches the data
That every step from raw data to result is captured and re-runnable
questions.explanation: A reproducible workflow documents and codifies each step so anyone can regenerate the outputs from the inputs.

questions.q: In data quality, what does 'completeness' measure?
options: The extent to which required values are present and not missing
questions.explanation: Completeness assesses whether all expected data points are present rather than missing or blank.

questions.q: What is the advantage of storing configuration (like file paths) in a separate config file rather than hardcoding it?
options: It lets the same code run in different environments without editing the code
It removes the need for version control
questions.explanation: Externalizing configuration means paths and settings can change per machine or user without altering the tested code itself.

questions.q: What is 'data lineage'?
options: The family who owns the data
The traceable path of data through its transformations from source to final output
The oldest record in a table
questions.explanation: Data lineage maps how data flows and changes across each pipeline stage, aiding debugging, auditing, and trust.

questions.q: Which naming practice best supports machine-readable, sortable filenames?
options: Lowercase words separated by underscores or hyphens, no spaces
questions.explanation: Avoiding spaces and special characters and using consistent separators prevents errors in scripts, URLs, and command lines.

questions.q: What does 'staging' typically refer to in a data pipeline?
options: An intermediate area where data is held and validated before loading into the target
questions.explanation: A staging area temporarily holds extracted data for cleaning and validation before it is loaded into the production destination.

questions.q: Why is it important to record the software and package versions used in an analysis?
options: Because results can change across versions, so recording them supports reproducibility
To make the analysis run faster
questions.explanation: Different software or library versions can produce different outputs, so capturing versions lets others recreate the exact environment.

questions.q: What is the main purpose of a 'controlled vocabulary' in data management?
options: To limit who can read the data
To standardize terms so the same concept is coded consistently
To translate data into other languages
questions.explanation: A controlled vocabulary fixes an agreed set of allowed terms, preventing inconsistencies like 'F', 'Female', and 'female' meaning the same thing.

questions.q: In data quality, 'consistency' refers to what?
options: How often data is backed up
Data agreeing across records and sources without contradiction
questions.explanation: Consistency means values do not contradict each other across a dataset or between linked datasets, e.g., a birth date matching a reported age.

questions.q: What is a 'repository' in Git terminology?
options: A storage location holding a project's files and their complete change history
questions.explanation: A Git repository contains all of a project's files together with the full history of commits tracking their changes.

questions.q: Why should archived datasets include their documentation and code alongside the data?
options: So future users can understand and reuse the data without external context
To prevent the data from being read
questions.explanation: Archiving data with its documentation, dictionary, and processing code ensures it remains interpretable and reusable long after the original team disperses.

questions.q: What does 'de-identification' of a dataset involve?
options: Removing or masking information that could identify individuals
questions.explanation: De-identification strips or masks direct and indirect identifiers so individuals cannot be readily recognized in the data.

questions.q: What is the benefit of using relative file paths instead of absolute paths in a project's scripts?
options: The project can be moved or shared and still run without editing paths
questions.explanation: Relative paths reference locations within the project folder, so the whole project runs on another machine without rewriting user-specific absolute paths.

questions.q: Which of these is a key element of a data management plan (DMP)?
options: How data will be collected, stored, documented, shared, and preserved
questions.explanation: A DMP describes the full data lifecycle (collection, storage, documentation, sharing, and long-term preservation) before a project begins.

questions.q: What does 'data validation' at the point of entry aim to prevent?
options: Invalid or out-of-range values from being recorded
questions.explanation: Entry-point validation enforces rules (e.g., age between 0 and 120) so bad values are caught immediately rather than during later cleaning.

questions.q: In Git, what does 'pull' do?
options: Fetches changes from a remote repository and merges them into your local copy
Uploads your commits to the server
questions.explanation: A pull retrieves updates from the remote repository and integrates them into your current local branch.

questions.q: Why is an audit trail (log of who changed what and when) important for data governance?
options: It supports accountability, error tracing, and compliance
It replaces the need for backups
questions.explanation: An audit trail records every access and change, enabling accountability, investigation of errors, and evidence of compliance.

questions.q: What is the risk of storing API keys or passwords directly in a script committed to Git?
options: Git will refuse to commit it
The secrets become part of the shared history and can be exposed
questions.explanation: Committed secrets persist in the repository history and can leak to anyone with access, so credentials should be kept in ignored config or environment variables.

questions.q: What does 'open data' mean?
options: Data that anyone can freely access, use, modify, and share, subject to at most attribution
questions.explanation: Open data can be freely accessed, reused, and redistributed by anyone, at most under requirements to attribute and share alike.

questions.q: When a bug is found in a data-cleaning script, what is the reproducibility advantage of having used code instead of manual edits?
options: You can fix the code and re-run to regenerate all corrected outputs consistently
questions.explanation: Because the process is codified, fixing the script and re-running it reliably reproduces the entire corrected pipeline, which manual edits cannot offer.
